idiom_name: discriminated union of node types + switch narrowing + never exhaustiveness check
implementation_notes: Discriminated unions plus switch narrowing are the TypeScript realization: a literal kind field discriminates the union, each case narrows to the node's fields, and a default branch assigning to never turns a missing case into a compile error. Keep the AST closed inside one project and let the compiler audit every evaluator; use classes implementing an interface when the node set must stay open to consumers.
pitfalls: The never check exists only where the default clause was written; a switch without it returns undefined for a new kind under strictNullChecks instead of failing.
Types are erased at run time: a node built from JSON is only as valid as the parser, so validate at the boundary rather than trusting the union.
Two node kinds sharing a discriminator value silently merge their cases; keep kind literals unique per node type.

variants.name: Interface with a class per grammar rule
variants.idiom_name: interface IExpression declaring interpret + one class per rule
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-union style, still common in OO codebases and in the classic pattern samples: an interface declaring interpret, one class per grammar rule implementing it. It reads like Java, supports instanceof handling and visitor-style double dispatch, and gives each rule a named type; in exchange node construction is verbose and the compiler cannot check that the set is complete.
pitfalls: private constructor parameters create fields implicitly; reordering parameters silently changes the public constructor signature.
instanceof survives compilation but compares class identity, so duplicated module copies break the checks.
No exhaustiveness: a missing rule shows up as a thrown abstract method call at run time, so cover the base method with a descriptive error.
